policy_title: Information, Education and Communication about Healthcare Needs
purpose:
This document sets out how {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} educates the patient and/or family in a language and format they can understand; how that education covers medicines and side effects when appropriate, food-drug interaction, diet, nutrition and immunisations, the specific disease process with complications and prevention, and preventing healthcare-associated infections; and how communication with patients and families is done effectively.

The chapter intent is that patients and families have a right to information, education and communication about their healthcare needs in a language and manner that is understood by them. A leaflet the patient cannot read, a discharge instruction that is only on the summary and never taught, or a once-at-admission talk that is never repeated when the plan changes, is not that intent.

This document is the education and communication method. Informing of rights at entry is PRE.1. The consent conversation is PRE.3. Follow-up advice on the discharge summary is AAC.8. Those remain those documents.
scope:
This policy applies to every point at which a patient or family at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} is taught about healthcare needs: out-patient, emergency after stabilisation, in-patient wards, day-care, intensive or high-dependency areas where they exist, and at discharge insofar as teaching happens. It binds the clinicians and nurses who educate, the person who checks that communication was effective, and the named lead who holds the method.

It covers: education in a language and format they can understand; education about safe and effective use of medication and potential side effects when appropriate; education about food-drug interaction, diet, nutrition and immunisations; education about the specific disease process, complications and prevention strategies; education about preventing healthcare-associated infections; and effective communication with patients and/or families.

Boundaries with other policies of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}:

- Awareness of rights and responsibilities at entry is governed by PRE.1. This document owns teaching about healthcare needs, not the rights charter.
- The consent conversation (procedure, risks, benefits, alternatives, who will perform, in a language they can understand) is PRE.3.b. This document owns ongoing education in that language. They may use the same language; they are not the same act.
- Discharge-summary follow-up advice in an understandable manner is governed by the discharge policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} (AAC.8). AAC.8 owns that the advice is on the paper the patient takes away and already hands teaching method to PRE. This document accepts that handoff. AAC.8 does not write how education is given during the stay.
- Safe and effective use of medication as an administration act is governed by MOM.6. Capture of near-miss, medication error and adverse drug reaction is MOM.7. This document owns teaching about medicines and side effects (PRE.4.b). MOM.7 still captures the event; teaching does not replace reporting.
- Nutritional-risk screen and therapeutic diet as a clinical act are governed by COP.13. Paediatric immunisation assessment is COP.8. Kitchen infection-control method is HIC.3. This document owns teaching about food-drug interaction, diet, nutrition and immunisations (PRE.4.c). It does not write the diet card, the immunisation schedule, or the kitchen SOP, and it does not name the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 in paragraph 2.
- Preventing healthcare-associated infections as an infection-prevention programme is governed by HIC.2, HIC.4 and HIC.5. This document owns teaching the patient and family how they can help prevent HAI (PRE.4.e). It does not rewrite bundles, surveillance or waste colours.
- Access to clinical records as a right is PRE.2.j. The record itself is IMS (not yet drafted). This document may use the record as a teaching aid; it does not grant or refuse access.
- Expected-cost explanation is PRE.5. This document does not teach the tariff.
policy_statement:
{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} educates the patient and/or family in a language and format that they can understand.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} educates the patient and/or family about the safe and effective use of medication and the potential side effects of the medication, when appropriate.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} educates the patient and/or family about food-drug interaction and about diet, nutrition and immunisations.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} educates the patient and/or family about their specific disease process, complications and prevention strategies.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} educates the patient and/or family about preventing healthcare-associated infections.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} communicates with patients and/or families effectively. A leaflet unread, or a monologue without a check that it was understood, is not effective communication.
procedure_steps:
1. Education in a language and format they can understand

Patient and/or family are educated in a language and format that they can understand.

How that language and format are chosen and recorded — spoken language, written material, interpreter or accompanying family as translator, and what is done when the patient cannot read — is [Hospital to define — how education language and format are chosen and recorded, including when the patient cannot read or does not share the staff's language]. A board or leaflet only in English, in a hospital whose patients do not read English, is not this OE. PRE.3.b uses the same language for the consent conversation; this step is ongoing education, not that conversation.

This document does not print a reading-age score or a named leaflet as a NABH mandate. Badarudeen and Sabharwal (2010) — chapter reference 1 — and Nouri and Rudd (2015) — chapter reference 14 — are used as frameworks for readability and oral health literacy, not as pasted protocols.

2. Education about medicines and potential side effects, when appropriate

Patient and/or family are educated about the safe and effective use of medication and the potential side effects of the medication, when appropriate.

When that education is given (for example at start of a medicine, at a change, or at discharge), what 'when appropriate' excludes, and how it is recorded, are [Hospital to define — when medication and side-effect education is given, what 'when appropriate' excludes, and how it is recorded]. Administration of the dose remains MOM.6. Capture of a near-miss, medication error or adverse drug reaction remains MOM.7; this teaching does not replace that report. This step does not print a side-effect list as a NABH mandate.

3. Education about food-drug interaction, diet, nutrition and immunisations

Patient and/or family are educated about food-drug interaction and about diet, nutrition and immunisations.

How that education is given for each of those topics this hospital actually uses, and how it is recorded, are [Hospital to define — how education on food-drug interaction, diet, nutrition and immunisations is given and recorded, including a recorded absence for a topic this hospital does not provide]. Nutritional-risk screen and therapeutic diet remain COP.13. Paediatric immunisation assessment remains COP.8. Kitchen method remains HIC.3. This step teaches; it does not write those methods. Unused immunisation as a service is a recorded absence against the service directory (AAC.1), not a copied immunisation SOP.

4. Education about the specific disease process, complications and prevention

Patient and/or family are educated about their specific disease process, complications and prevention strategies.

How that education is given for the conditions this hospital treats, and how it is recorded, are [Hospital to define — how disease-process, complication and prevention education is given and recorded]. Specific means the condition this patient has, not a generic 'be healthy' poster. Clinical diagnosis and the care plan remain AAC.3; this step is the teaching about that diagnosis.

5. Education about preventing healthcare-associated infections

Patient and/or family are educated about preventing healthcare associated infections.

How that education is given — what the patient and family are asked to do (for example hand hygiene, not touching devices, telling staff of fever) — and how it is recorded, are [Hospital to define — how patients and families are educated about preventing healthcare-associated infections, and how that is recorded]. Bundles, surveillance, isolation and waste remain HIC.2, HIC.4 and HIC.5. This step does not rewrite those methods and does not name Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 in paragraph 2.

6. Communication with patients and/or families is done effectively

Communication with the patients and/or families is done effectively. This step is the documented-evidence anchor of an Excellence requirement the standard asterisks. An assessor will ask not whether a leaflet exists, but whether the conversation worked. The answer must be a method this hospital uses to check understanding and to adapt when it did not, not a stack of unreadable printouts counted as communication.

The reason this is written separately from steps 1-5 is that those steps name topics. This step names quality. A medicine talk in a language the family does not speak, a disease explanation that the patient nods through and cannot repeat, or a discharge teaching that is only a signature on AAC.8's summary, is education that was not communication. The chapter intent is language and manner that are understood. The common error is to treat 'we told them' as 'they understood', or to copy an EDUCATE checklist as if NABH had mandated that model.

Marcus (2014) — chapter reference 11, EDUCATE — and Ha and Longnecker (2010) — chapter reference 7 — are the book's own sources on verbal education and doctor-patient communication. They are used as frameworks for what 'effectively' can mean (teach-back, chunking, checking understanding, adapting to distress). They are not pasted as a protocol, and they are not a mandate to print those acronyms on the form. Readability work in the same bibliography (Badarudeen and Sabharwal 2010; Roberts, Zhang and Dyer 2016; Williams, Muir and Rosdahl 2016) informs written material at step 1; this step is the oral exchange Nouri and Rudd (2015) name.

How communication is done so that it is effective — who speaks, how understanding is checked, what is done when it was not understood, and how that is recorded — is [Hospital to define — how communication with patients and families is done effectively, including how understanding is checked and what is done when it was not]. Effective communication applies to every topic in steps 1-5 and to the teaching AAC.8 requires on the discharge summary. A harvested signature is not a check of understanding.

This document does not print a communication script, a minimum number of minutes, or a named model as a NABH mandate.

7. Records, review and the order of operations

The language-and-format method, topic education records, and the effective-communication method, are retrievable against the unique identification number where teaching was given.

The quality or accreditation coordinator audits a sample of these records at [Hospital to define — the audit interval for patient-education and communication records] for: language and format they can understand; medicines and side effects when appropriate; food-drug, diet, nutrition and immunisations as this hospital provides them; disease process; preventing HAI; a check that communication was effective rather than a leaflet or a signature alone; and no restatement of MOM.6, MOM.7, COP.13, COP.8 or HIC method offered as this education.

This policy is reviewed at [Hospital to define — the review interval for this policy], and sooner when a family left unable to repeat the teaching, or a leaflet-only process was offered as communication, or when AAC.8, MOM.6, MOM.7, COP.13, COP.8 or HIC documents that this document hands work to are revised.
responsibility:
The head of the institution is accountable for {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} educating patients and families about healthcare needs in a language and format they can understand, and for communication being effective.

The named lead for patient education and communication authors and keeps current the language-and-format method, the topic methods and the effective-communication method. The named lead is [Hospital to define — the named lead for patient education and communication].

Clinicians and nurses who teach apply those methods. Staff who hand a leaflet without checking understanding do not meet step 6.

The quality or accreditation coordinator audits the records at step 7 and reports findings to the head of the institution.

All staff are expected to treat unread material, teaching in a language the family does not use, and a signature offered as proof of understanding, as defects, and to report them.
references_text:
- National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare Providers (NABH), Standards for Small Healthcare Organisations, 3rd Edition — Patient Rights and Education chapter, standard PRE.4.
- Badarudeen, S., & Sabharwal, S. (2010). Assessing readability of patient education materials. Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research, 468(10), 2572-2580 — chapter reference 1; used as a framework for written material; not pasted as a protocol.
- Marcus, C. (2014). Strategies for improving the quality of verbal patient and family education: a review of the literature and creation of the EDUCATE model. Health Psychology and Behavioral Medicine, 2(1), 482-495 — chapter reference 11; used as a framework for effective verbal education; not pasted as a protocol.
- Nouri, S. S., & Rudd, R. E. (2015). Health literacy in the "oral exchange". Patient Education and Counseling, 98(5), 565-571 — chapter reference 14; used as a framework for oral understanding; not pasted as a protocol.
- Ha, J. F., & Longnecker, N. (2010). Doctor-patient communication: a review. Ochsner Journal, 10(1), 38-43 — chapter reference 7; used as a framework; not pasted as a protocol.
- Internal documents of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}: the language-and-format method; topic education methods; the effective-communication method; the rights, consent, discharge, medication-administration, medication-error, nutrition, immunisation, infection-prevention and information-management policies.
distribution:
Controlled master copy: office of the head of the institution, {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}, with the quality or accreditation coordinator.

Copies issued to: out-patient; emergency; in-patient wards; ICU where it exists; nursing administration; and the named lead.

The current version is available to all staff at [Hospital to define — intranet location or nursing station folder]. The education methods — the working documents this policy requires — are held where teaching is given.

Superseded versions are withdrawn from all points of use on issue of a revision, and one dated copy of each is retained by the quality or accreditation coordinator.
abbreviations:
Abbreviations already defined in the HIC.1 to HIC.6 master policies are not repeated here. A reader using this document on its own should refer to those policies for the shared glossary, including NABH, SHCO, OE, WHO, SOP, PPE and HAI.

The following abbreviations are used in this document and are not defined in HIC.1 to HIC.6:

HAI — healthcare-associated infection (also in HIC; repeated here because PRE.4.e names it)
IMS — Information Management System (NABH chapter; not yet drafted)

Any additional abbreviation used locally within {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} is [Hospital to define] and is added to this list at the next revision.
disclaimer:
This document is a template prepared for the guidance of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} and must be reviewed, adapted and formally approved by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} before use. Every entry marked [Hospital to define] must be replaced with the hospital's own decision; a document issued with those markers left in place is not an approved policy.

The requirements in this document are accreditation requirements of the NABH SHCO 3rd Edition rather than duties under a named Act of Parliament. In particular those arising under no named Act of Parliament; the duties in this document are accreditation requirements of the NABH SHCO 3rd Edition are written here as accreditation method, not as a copied statute. This policy does not import the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010, or the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 as a checklist. Statutory duties that arise under other documents of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} remain those documents. {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} is responsible for verifying any statutory duty that applies to it; this document does not constitute legal advice.

The clinical and technical content reflects recognised national and international guidance current at the date of preparation. {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} remains responsible for verifying that it is current and consistent with the edition of the accreditation standard against which it is being assessed.

This document is not issued by, endorsed by, or affiliated with NABH, the World Health Organization, the National Centre for Disease Control, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, any Pollution Control Board, or any other body named in it. Wording is original; no text has been reproduced from the standards, rules or guidelines referenced.
